title: Haman's Decree: A Day Set for Destruction
summary: King Xerxes promotes Haman the Agagite above all his officials and commands everyone to bow to him, but Mordecai refuses. Enraged to learn that Mordecai is a Jew, Haman resolves to destroy all the Jews in the empire, casts the lot (pur) to choose a day, and persuades the king to authorize the slaughter of an unnamed people whose laws are different. Letters sealed with the king's ring go out to every province ordering the killing of all Jews on the thirteenth of Adar, and while the king and Haman sit down to drink, the city of Susa is thrown into confusion.
story: Chapter 2 ended with Mordecai saving the king's life and receiving nothing. Chapter 3 opens, with bitter irony, with someone else being promoted: Haman, of whom nothing has been said before. The conflict between Mordecai and Haman is the engine of the rest of the book. Esther is queen, but her Jewish identity is still hidden, and she does not appear in this chapter at all. Its closing picture, the king and Haman drinking while the city is bewildered, sets up the crisis that chapter 4 must answer: will Esther use her position to save her people?
historical:
The lot is cast in the first month, Nisan, of Xerxes' twelfth year (verse 7), about 474 BC, five years after Esther became queen. It falls on the twelfth month, Adar, nearly a year away. Ancient readers would have seen this long delay as a disastrous choice for Haman, since it left time for a response.

Haman's offer of ten thousand talents of silver (verse 9) was a staggering sum. A talent was a heavy weight of metal, and the amount would have been a large fraction of the whole empire's annual revenue. Haman probably expected to recover it from the plunder of the Jews' property (verse 13). The Persian postal system, with mounted couriers stationed at intervals along the royal roads, was famous in the ancient world for speed, and it carried the decree to every province. Satraps were the governors of the empire's great regions, and beneath them were provincial governors and local officials (verse 12).
cultural:
Bowing before a superior was ordinary courtesy in the ancient Near East, and Israelites bowed to kings and to one another without any sense of idolatry (for example 2 Samuel 14:4 and 1 Kings 1:16). Mordecai's refusal therefore needs an explanation, which the text only hints at: when asked, he tells the servants that he is a Jew (verse 4). The key may lie in Haman's ancestry. He is an Agagite, which most readers connect with Agag, king of the Amalekites (1 Samuel 15). The Amalekites had attacked Israel after the exodus, and God had declared lasting war against them (Exodus 17:8-16; Deuteronomy 25:17-19). Saul, son of Kish of Benjamin, had been told to destroy them and had spared Agag. Mordecai, also a Benjaminite descended from Kish (2:5), now faces a descendant of Agag.

Casting lots to find a favorable day was a normal practice in the ancient world, where people believed the gods revealed propitious times through such methods. The word pur is related to an Akkadian word for lot, and archaeologists have found an inscribed clay die from Assyria called by that term. The signet ring (verse 10) carried the king's seal; handing it to Haman gave him authority to issue decrees in the king's name. The decree was issued on the thirteenth of Nisan (verse 12), the day before Passover, the feast when Israel remembered God's deliverance from a foreign king who had tried to destroy them.
literary: The chapter is built on dramatic irony and escalation. A personal slight becomes a plan for genocide in a single verse (verse 6). Haman's speech to the king (verses 8-9) is a masterpiece of manipulation: he never names the Jews, mixes a half-truth (their laws are different) with a lie (they do not obey the king's laws), and appeals to the king's interests and treasury. The king does not even ask which people he is condemning. The chapter's closing verse sets two scenes side by side with devastating effect: “Then the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was in confusion.” The language of the decree, “to destroy, kill, and annihilate” (verse 13), will be repeated almost word for word in the counter-decree of chapter 8, part of the book's pattern of reversal.

outline.t: Haman is promoted, and Mordecai refuses to bow
Haman resolves to destroy all the Jews
The lot is cast for the day of destruction
The decree is written, sealed, and sent

doctrines.note: Haman's wounded pride turns into murderous hatred of an entire people (verses 5-6). The chapter traces how personal resentment, given power, can become systematic evil written into law.

Haman casts the lot to find a lucky day, but Proverbs 16:33 teaches that though the lot is cast into the lap, its decision comes from the LORD. The lot falls almost a year away, giving time for deliverance. The book never states this, but it invites readers to see who really governs the outcome.

Haman's plan targets the whole people of God, the descendants of Abraham to whom God had promised a future and through whom he had promised to bless the nations. A threat to the Jews was a threat to God's promises themselves.

words.note: Pur, lot. The narrator explains this foreign word for his readers (verse 7), and it gives its name to the festival of Purim (9:26). Haman uses the lot to choose the day for destruction, but the festival named after it celebrates deliverance, a reversal built into the very name.

Agagi, Agagite. The word identifies Haman's ancestry and most likely connects him with Agag, the Amalekite king whom Saul failed to destroy (1 Samuel 15). The title recurs through the book (3:1, 10; 8:3, 5; 9:24), keeping the old enmity between Israel and Amalek in view.

Shamad, to destroy or exterminate. The verb describes Haman's intent to wipe out Mordecai's people (verse 6) and appears in the decree (verse 13). It is the language of total annihilation, which makes the later reversal all the more complete.

Shachah, to bow down. The same verb is used for bowing to people and for worshiping God. Mordecai's refusal to bow to Haman (verses 2 and 5) is the spark of the whole conflict, and the word's range leaves readers to consider what it meant for Mordecai to withhold it.

christ: Haman's plan to destroy the Jews is one of many moments in the Bible when the line of promise is threatened: Pharaoh's order to kill the Hebrew boys (Exodus 1), Athaliah's attempt to wipe out David's royal family (2 Kings 11), and later Herod's slaughter of the infants of Bethlehem (Matthew 2:16). Christians have read these as part of one long conflict between God's purpose and the powers that oppose it, a conflict that reaches its climax at the cross and resurrection. The New Testament itself does not cite Esther, and the link is thematic. It is also worth noticing that the decree is issued on the eve of Passover, the feast Jesus would later celebrate with his disciples on the night he was betrayed, when he interpreted his coming death as the true deliverance of God's people (Luke 22:14-20).

hard.q: Why did Mordecai refuse to bow to Haman, when Israelites bowed to kings and officials elsewhere in the Bible?
hard.a:
The Hebrew text does not directly say why. Several explanations have been offered. One is that Haman demanded honor that belonged only to God, perhaps as part of Persian court practice, which the Greeks regarded as treating the king almost as divine. The Greek additions to Esther, found in the Septuagint, include a prayer of Mordecai saying that he refused so as not to set the glory of a human being above the glory of God. A second explanation is ethnic and historical: as a Benjaminite of Saul's family, Mordecai would not bow to a descendant of Agag, the Amalekite enemy of Israel. A third view sees stubborn pride on Mordecai's part, noting that his refusal endangered his whole people.

The text's only clue is that Mordecai explained his refusal by saying he was a Jew (verse 4), which suggests a reason rooted in his identity and faith rather than personal dislike. The first two explanations can be combined, and many interpreters do so. What the book makes clear is that Haman's response, to plan the destruction of an entire people for one man's refusal, is monstrous whatever Mordecai's motives were.

questions: Haman described the Jews as a people whose laws are different and who are not in the king's interest. How are minorities still described in ways that make their mistreatment seem reasonable?
The king authorized mass killing without even asking which people it was. What responsibility do those in power have to know the consequences of what they sign?
Mordecai's refusal to bow was tied to his identity as a Jew. Where might faithfulness to God require you to stand apart, and how do you tell conviction from mere stubbornness?
